| [LIT-384](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-384.md) | The somatic marker hypothesis and the possible functions of the prefrontal cortex | Damasio (1996), DOI-10.1098/rstb.1996.0125. States the somatic marker hypothesis: ventromedial prefrontal cortex holds learned links between classes of situation and the body states (emotions) that went with them; when a situation recurs, those states are re-enacted, through the body or through an "as if" loop in somatosensory cortex, and mark imagined option-outcome pairs as good or bad, overtly as a feeling or covertly as a bias, so that reasoning works over a pruned space. Evidence summarised: ventromedial patients with intact intellect decide badly in life, lack skin-conductance responses to emotive pictures, and in the gambling task keep choosing the losing decks and show no anticipatory responses. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-332](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-332.md)); worth reading as the shortest statement of the somatic marker hypothesis by its author, with the evidence it then rested on. It is a hypothesis paper: the mechanism (ventromedial prefrontal linkages that re-enact body states, by a "body loop" or an "as if body loop", which then mark options good or bad) is stated, not shown, and the evidence it reports is lesion and skin-conductance work summarised from other papers, without numbers. Its strongest piece, that ventromedial patients lack anticipatory skin-conductance responses in the gambling task while responding normally to the losses themselves, is reported here in one paragraph; the 1997 Science report filed alongside it is the place to see that result. Whether the account is true is not this note's question. |

| [LIT-388](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-388.md) | The nature of feelings: evolutionary and neurobiological origins | Damasio & Carvalho (2013), Nature Reviews Neuroscience 14:143–152. Feelings are mental experiences of body states, and they report homeostatic value: a valenced read-out of interoceptive maps that lets an organism learn and anticipate what restores or threatens its physiology. The first integrated whole-body maps are in the upper brainstem (parabrachial nucleus, periaqueductal grey, deep superior colliculus); the insula refines feeling but is not needed for it, since a patient with both insulae destroyed still feels pain, pleasure, hunger and compassion. The authors propose, without evidence of their own, that feeling starts in unmyelinated interoceptive fibres open to ions and ligands along their length. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-330](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-330.md)); worth reading as the shortest statement of Damasio's account of feeling as the felt read-out of homeostatic body maps, with its two empirical planks: patients whose insulae are destroyed still feel, and the upper brainstem is where whole-body interoceptive maps first assemble. It is an Opinion piece with no new data. The systems-level case rests on lesion and stimulation evidence it cites; the cellular proposal (unmyelinated interoceptive fibres and ephaptic coupling as the root of sentience) is offered as a hypothesis and stays one. |

| [LIT-432](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-432.md) | The Emotion Machine: Commonsense Thinking, Artificial Intelligence, and the Future of the Human Mind | Minsky (2006), Simon & Schuster, read in the author's 2005 draft. | [LIT-462](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-462.md) | The Self and the Future | Williams (1970), DOI-10.2307/2183946. One experiment, told twice. A and B enter a machine that exchanges their memories and characters, and choose selfishly which emerging person gets $100,000 and which torture: the outcomes make "changing bodies" the natural description. Told as a series of things that will happen to me (amnesia, changed character, another's "memories", then torture), fear stays rational at every step, and the step that completes the swap changes only what happens to someone else. Undecidability and convention make the clash worse, not better. If forced to choose selfishly, pass the pain to the other body, and call it a "risk". | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-387](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-387.md)), in a JSTOR copy of the published article posted on a University of Vermont course page; worth reading as the strongest case that first-person concern tracks the body, and the paper that made the reduplication-free body swap a problem for the psychological view. It tells one body-exchange experiment twice. Told third-personally, with choices before and reactions after, it says A and B swap bodies. Told first-personally, as a series of things that will happen to me before I am tortured, it says I am the one tortured. It argues that neither indeterminacy nor convention can resolve the clash, and ends with a "rather shaky" preference for the bodily answer, as a "risk". An argument from what fear is rational, not a theory. |

| [LIT-540](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-540.md) | Impulsive action: emotional impulses and their control | Frijda, Ridderinkhof & Rietveld (2014), Frontiers in Psychology 5:518. Appraisal of an event's pertinence to one's concerns elicits a state of action readiness, a motive to change one's relation to the object, which has "control precedence". Modes of action readiness correspond to emotions (hostility to anger, avoidance to fear). Much emotion regulation is itself one state of action readiness checking another, so "there is no clear distinction between processes of emotion and processes of emotion regulation". | [LIT-542](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-542.md) | The theory of constructed emotion: an active inference account of interoception and categorization | Barrett (2017), SCAN 12(1):1–23. The brain runs an internal model of the body in the world for allostasis. Its predictions are "concepts" issued from agranular limbic cortex and refined by prediction error. The brain's core task is allostasis, run through an internal model whose predictions are "concepts". An instance of emotion is what happens when the brain categorizes predicted interoceptive and exteroceptive sensation with an emotion concept. On this account emotion categories have no neural "essences", and causal appraisal theories are "highly doubtful". The paper is a theoretical synthesis: its own data are a few figures, and the rest is cited evidence and explicitly labelled hypotheses. |

People and other animals discount delayed rewards hyperbolically, so preferences reverse as a smaller, sooner reward comes near, and a person becomes a population of reward-seeking "interests" that must forestall one another. Worth reading as the shortest complete statement of picoeconomics in Ainslie's own words. Hyperbolic discounting makes preference reverse as a smaller, sooner reward draws near, so a person behaves like a population of "interests" that bargain across time. Will is not a faculty above them but a recursive self-prediction: treating each choice as a precedent "bundles" future rewards, an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma in which "credibility is power". | [LIT-1263](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1263.md) v2 | Interoceptive inference, emotion, and the embodied self | Seth (2013), Trends in Cognitive Sciences 17(11):565–573, an Opinion article. Emotions are "interoceptive inference": felt states are the content of hierarchical top-down predictions of the causes of interoceptive signals, compared with bottom-up prediction errors in the anterior insula. Prediction errors are also cancelled by action, as descending predictions set the reference points of autonomic reflexes, the visceral counterpart of active inference in motor control. The same scheme is applied to the experience of body ownership. The rubber hand illusion is a revision of the multisensory self-model under precision-weighted error. Low interoceptive sensitivity goes with greater susceptibility to it, and a virtual hand pulsing in time with the heartbeat is owned more. No direct test of the model is claimed. | Active — read in full 2026-10-19 ([NOTE-1000](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1000.md)); worth reading as the short statement that put emotion and body ownership under one predictive-coding mechanism: felt emotion is the content of top-down predictions of the causes of interoceptive signals, the anterior insula is the comparator, and the experience of body ownership is what the brain infers to be "most likely to be me" from interoceptive and exteroceptive signals together. It is an opinion article with no new data. Its evidence is indirect and cited, and its one figure is a study by the author's own group, an augmented-reality rubber hand illusion whose virtual hand flashed in or out of time with the heartbeat. The record's bridge from its interoception cluster to body ownership. |
| [LIT-1270](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1270.md) | Is the folk concept of pain polyeidic? | Borg, Harrison, Stazicker & Salomons (2019/2020), Mind & Language 35(1):29–47. Experimental philosophers (Sytsma, Reuter and others) argue that the folk think of pains as bodily, not mental, because lay participants deny pains privacy, subjectivity and incorrigibility. Borg et al. raise six objections. The samples are small and skewed; only acute pain was probed; asking whether pain is "in the mind" carries a pejorative implicature; means sit near neutral; denying Cartesian marks shows at most a non-Cartesian mental view; and the data support only a partly bodily concept. Pilot vignettes of their own (damage that never hurt) drew mind-centred answers (means 5.70 and 5.79 on a disagree-high scale). They propose that the folk concept of pain is "polyeidic": an amalgam of dimensions (mental/bodily, public/private, conscious/unconscious, aversive, purposeful, motivational) on which people hold latent, framing-sensitive positions, with possible uses in clinical communication. | Active — read in full 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-994](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-994.md)) from the "revise and resubmit" manuscript in Reading's CentAUR repository; worth reading as the clearest statement of the case against the experimental philosophers' "bodily view" of pain (Sytsma, Reuter and colleagues), and as a proposal that the folk concept is "polyeidic": several dimensions, mental/bodily among them, along which judgements move with framing. Four of its six objections are methodological (samples, acute pain only, the loaded "in the mind" probe, means near neutral), and two are structural: the data fit a non-Cartesian mental view as well, and they show at most that the concept is in part bodily. Read it as argument, not data. Its own evidence is two pilot vignettes reported in a footnote, with means and no sample size, and the polyeidic view is a research programme without a test. It is folk-concept evidence and does not bear on the record's rubber hand THEORYs. |
| [LIT-1353](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1353.md) v2 | The Theory of Constructed Emotion: More Than a Feeling | Barrett et al. (2025). A reply to van Heijst et al., who proposed that basic emotion theory explains emotions as bodily states and the theory of constructed emotion explains the feelings that arise from them. The authors argue that this split misrepresents constructed emotion through three simplifications, and that the two theories rest on incommensurate assumptions and cannot be reconciled. | Active — read in full 2026-10-22 ([NOTE-1067](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1067.md)) from the publisher's text in PubMed Central (PMC12164598, CC BY-NC 4.0); worth reading as the theory's architects saying plainly that feeling is not a second phenomenon that represents the body's regulation: the same allostatic signals that regulate the body make feeling, an instance of emotion is one whole-brain event, and splitting it into an objective bodily state and a subjective feeling is a premise of basic emotion theory, which they call incommensurable with theirs. It is a reply with no data; its evidence is cited lists, much of it from the authors' own groups, and basic emotion theory is described by its opponents. It does not discuss emotion regulation, reappraisal or therapy. |
| [LIT-1359](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1359.md) v2 | A systems identification approach using Bayes factors to deconstruct the brain bases of emotion regulation | Bo, Kraynak, Kwon, Sun, Gianaros & Wager (2024). Across two fMRI studies (n = 182 and 176), Bayes factors identify four reappraisal-related systems: an anterior prefrontal one selective for reappraisal, a fronto-parietal-insular one engaged by reappraisal and emotion generation alike, a largely subcortical one (amygdala, hypothalamus, periaqueductal gray) active in negative emotion but unaffected by reappraisal, and a posterior cortical one downregulated by it. | Active — read in full 2026-10-22 ([NOTE-1061](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1061.md)) from the bioRxiv preprint, version 2 (10 May 2023), not the closed version of record; worth reading as the first imaging study of reappraisal large enough (n = 182 and 176, replicated in both) to give evidence for nulls, which lets it say which regions are engaged only by regulating, which are shared with generating negative emotion, and which emotion-responsive regions reappraisal leaves unchanged. Most of the reappraisal network is shared with generation, a smaller anterior prefrontal and temporo-parietal set is selective for it, and every subcortical emotion-responsive region, amygdala and PAG included, was unchanged while reported negative affect fell. One instructed strategy, one picture task, BOLD means and one rating per trial; its talk of "subcortical-level affective experience" goes beyond what was measured. |
| [LIT-1405](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1405.md) | How Does Intergroup Contact Reduce Prejudice? Meta-Analytic Tests of Three Mediators | Pettigrew & Tropp (2008). Tests meta-analytically the three most studied mediators of contact's effect on prejudice: knowledge about the outgroup, reduced anxiety about intergroup contact, and increased empathy and perspective taking. All three mediate, but knowledge appears less strong than anxiety reduction and empathy. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-23, not read. Registered from the owner's exchange of 2026-10-22, "Ben Franklin Effect Explained". No NOTE is filed. |
| [LIT-1433](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1433.md) | Demystifying Emotions: A Typology of Theories in Psychology and Philosophy | Moors (2022), Cambridge University Press. A typology of emotion theories in psychology (evolutionary, network, appraisal, goal-directed, psychological constructionist, social) and philosophy (feeling, judgmental, quasi-judgmental, perceptual, embodied, motivational), compared with tools from the philosophy of science. It also proposes Moors's own skeptical "goal-directed theory", "based on the central idea that all kinds of behaviors and feelings are grounded in goal-striving". Unread beyond the front matter: the theory is read in her 2017 article [LIT-1434](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1434.md). | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-23 from Crossref and the publisher's free front matter, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. OpenAlex lists the book as closed, with no repository copy; Cambridge Core offers no open chapter; no Lirias or author-posted copy was found. The front matter and table of contents, which Cambridge hosts openly, were read. Filed as the book-length statement of Moors's goal-directed theory of emotion, the theory whose 2017 article ([LIT-1434](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1434.md)) is the nearest prior statement of the record's reading of appraisal as negotiation. Its Chapter 7, on response evaluation theories and her goal-directed theory, is the part to read first. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-1434](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1434.md) | The power of goal-directed processes in the causation of emotional and other actions | Moors, Boddez & De Houwer (2017), Emotion Review 9(4):310–318. Standard dual-process models make stimulus-driven processes the default and give goal-directed ones a late, regulatory role, in action research and in emotion research alike. The authors reverse the default. Goal-directed processes, which select the action option with the highest expected utility, can be fast and automatic too, so most of the competition that decides behaviour is between goal-directed processes, settled by the values and expectancies of outcomes. Emotional action tendencies can be caused this way. Appraisal-to-action-tendency links are sophisticated stimulus-driven processes. Evidence for stimulus-driven control rests on null results open to hidden goals. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1117](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1117.md)): in full, from the submitted manuscript deposited in Ghent University's repository. Worth reading as the shortest statement of Moors's goal-directed account of emotional action, and as the nearest prior statement of the record's reading of appraisal as negotiation. Goal-directed processes, which weigh the utility of action options by the values and expectancies of their outcomes, are the default cause of action, emotional action included. Most of the competition that decides behaviour is between goal-directed processes, and its winner is fixed by values and expectancies. Control precedence is what high goal relevance produces, so an emotional episode is a decision process with higher stakes. The competition is run on a common currency, expected utility, which is the point where the record parts from it. |
| [LIT-1436](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1436.md) | Toward an integrative psychometric model of emotions | Lange, Dalege, Borsboom, van Kleef & Fischer (2020), Perspectives on Psychological Science 15(2):444–468. An integrative psychometric model of emotions must allow distinct emotions (affect-program theories), variation between and within persons (constructionist theories) and causal relations among components (appraisal theories). Reflective and formative latent-variable models do not; a psychometric network model, in which "the network constitutes the emotion", does. Distinct emotions are weakly emergent small-world communities of components. Strongly connected networks sustain their own activation, which predicts hysteresis and longer emotions. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1098](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1098.md)): in part, from the published version (CC BY-NC) deposited in the University of Amsterdam's repository. Worth reading as the proposal that an emotion is a network of causally interacting components, the move Borsboom made for mental disorders ([LIT-547](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-547.md)) applied to emotion. Affect-program, constructionist and appraisal theories each demand one property: distinct emotions, variation between and within persons, and causal relations among components. Reflective and formative latent-variable models fail at least one. A network model meets all three, with a distinct emotion as a weakly emergent small-world community. Strong connectivity predicts self-sustaining activation and hysteresis, so longer emotions. The persistence it gives is a network state's, not an ordering's, and the model is unsigned. |
| [LIT-1437](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1437.md) | The World of Emotions is not Two-Dimensional | Fontaine, Scherer, Roesch & Ellsworth (2007), Psychological Science 18(12):1050–1057. Against two-dimensional valence–arousal models: in three languages, four dimensions are needed to represent the meaning of emotion words, rated on 144 features covering six emotion components. In order of importance they are evaluation-pleasantness, potency-control, activation-arousal and unpredictability. Unread: known from the abstract and from later papers of the same group. | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-23 from Crossref, not read: a lawful copy exists but this client could not reach it. The University of Geneva's Archive ouverte holds the published version (unige:97776) restricted to UNIGE/HUG users. The University of Reading's repository (CentAUR, eprint 30302) and Ghent University's bibliography (418787) list it without a public full text. The SAGE PDF refused this client behind a bot check, and the Geneva E3 Lab's publications page does not post it. A web search found no author or course posting. OpenAlex points to a CiteSeerX cache, which was not used because its source could not be traced. Its four dimensions are read from the PubMed abstract, and its "potency-control" dimension is glossed as "dominance" by Shuman, Sander and Scherer ([LIT-1458](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1458.md)). Filed because the record renamed its "dominance" to "potential" to avoid the PAD homonym, and this is the study that places the PAD axis among the component process model's dimensions. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-1438](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1438.md) | The current status of research on the structure of evaluative space | Norris, Gollan, Berntson & Cacioppo (2010), Biological Psychology 84(3):422–436. A review of the evaluative space model. The affect system has separable positive and negative channels whose joint output is a bipolar predisposition to approach or avoid. They can be activated reciprocally, independently or together. Coactivation, simultaneous or by fast oscillation, is ambivalence, rare and arousing. Asymmetric activation functions give a negativity bias and a positivity offset, and recalibrate with context. Levels of the neuraxis can override one another. Clinical implications for depression and anxiety. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1101](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1101.md)): in full, from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC2894997, NIHMS165251). Worth reading as the evaluative space model's own later summary, written with Berntson and Cacioppo. Positivity and negativity are separable systems, whose combined output is a bipolar predisposition to approach or withdraw. They can be activated reciprocally, independently or together, and coactivation is ambivalence. Ambivalence and neutrality give the same middling output from different underlying states. Negativity has the higher gain and positivity the higher intercept. It stands in for the unread 1994 and 1997 papers ([LIT-1453](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1453.md), [LIT-1456](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1456.md)). |
| [LIT-1440](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1440.md) | Induction and Profiling of Strong Multi-Componential Emotions in Virtual Reality | Meuleman & Rudrauf (2021), IEEE Trans. Affective Computing 12:189–202 (online 2018). Passive induction yields weak emotions that do not engage all components, so componential hypotheses cannot be tested with it. In VR, 53 participants played seven games (154 balanced observations) and rated componential items after each. Item clustering gave fear and joy clusters spanning appraisal, motivation, physiology, feeling and regulation. Appraisal predicted fear and joy intensity best. Game differences in fear were absorbed by appraisal and regulation, subject differences in joy were not. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1097](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1097.md)): in full, from the authors' accepted manuscript in the Archive ouverte UNIGE (unige:112041). Worth reading as an argument, with data, that passive induction (pictures, film) cannot test componential hypotheses such as synchronization, because it does not engage all components, and that virtual reality can. 53 participants played seven commercial VR games and rated appraisal, motivation, physiology, feeling and regulation items after each. Clustering found multi-componential fear and joy patterns, and appraisal items predicted fear and joy intensity best. Componentiality is assessed across observations, one retrospective self-report per game. Nothing is measured within an episode, and there is no synchronization index. |
| [LIT-1441](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1441.md) | Origins and functions of positive and negative affect: A control-process view | Carver & Scheier (1990), Psychological Review 97(1):19–35. The paper usually cited for the control-process account of affect: a second feedback loop monitors the rate at which the action loop reduces its discrepancy, and affect is that loop's error signal, positive when progress beats a reference rate and negative when it falls short. Unread: the account is read in Carver's 2018 restatement ([LIT-1449](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1449.md)). | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-23 from Crossref, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. Looked for on 2026-10-23. Unpaywall reports no open copy. The journal (APA, Psychological Review) is closed. A web search found the APA record, DeepDyve (paid), ERIC (EJ494079, record only), a Widener University file that is a reference list citing it, and Carnegie Mellon's KiltHub record of a later Carver and Scheier chapter (2012, no file attached). The only full text seen was an author upload on ResearchGate, which this record does not use. Europe PMC has no open copy of it or of any other Carver statement of the model before 2018. The model is read first-hand, briefly, in Carver's 2018 author manuscript in PubMed Central ([LIT-1449](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1449.md)), which restates that affect tracks the velocity of goal attainment against a reference value. Filed for the record's account of valence as an ordering serving as the negotiation's potential ([CLAIM-440](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-440.md)), whose sign clause this paper anticipates. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-1443](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1443.md) | A Multi-Componential Approach to Emotion Recognition and the Effect of Personality | Mohammadi & Vuilleumier (2022), IEEE Trans. Affective Computing 13:1127–1139 (online 2020). Crowdworkers rated 39 CoreGRID items and 10 discrete emotions after watching film clips (1,567 surveys, 99 clips). Clustering of emotion profiles in componential space separates positive from negative, then five clusters. PCA gives six dimensions beyond valence and arousal. Ordinal regression on all components predicts discrete-emotion ratings best; no single component suffices. Personality correlates more with componential items than with feelings or discrete emotions. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1118](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1118.md)): in full, from the authors' arXiv preprint (2010.11370v1, October 2020). Worth reading only as the behavioural groundwork for the later fMRI study ([LIT-1444](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1444.md)). Crowdworkers rated 39 CoreGRID items and 10 discrete emotions after whole film clips (1,567 surveys, 99 clips). Six principal components emerged (action tendency, pleasant feeling, novelty, norms, arousal, goal relevance). Ordinal regression from all components predicted discrete-emotion ratings better than any single component. Personality traits correlated with componential items more than with feelings. It does not mention synchronization and measures nothing within an episode. |
| [LIT-1444](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1444.md) | Brain networks subserving functional core processes of emotions identified with componential modeling | Mohammadi, Van De Ville & Vuilleumier (2023), Cerebral Cortex 33:7993–8010. Twenty participants watched 40 film clips during fMRI and rated 119 salient events (12 s each) on 32 CoreGRID features, and heart and respiration rate were recorded. Partial least squares correlation between event-wise brain maps and feature ratings yields six latent variables, the "functional core processes": valuation (wanting-like), novelty, hedonic impact (liking-like), goal monitoring, caring for others ("being moved") and approach/avoidance. No arousal process emerges, and the processes mix components rather than mapping one to one. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1107](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1107.md)): in full, from the published version (CC BY 4.0) in the Archive ouverte UNIGE (unige:170302). Worth reading as the first attempt to recover the component process model's components from brain and behaviour together. Twenty participants watched 40 film clips during fMRI and then rated 119 salient 12-second events on 32 CoreGRID features. Heart and respiration rate were recorded. Partial least squares correlation found six brain–behaviour latent variables, read as valuation, novelty, hedonic impact, goal monitoring, caring for others and approach/avoidance. For the record, the result is two distinct valence-like networks: a "wanting"-like valuation process and a "liking"-like hedonic one. Each event gets a feature vector, but no within-episode synchronization is computed. |
| [LIT-1445](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1445.md) | Pleasure as a sign you can attend to something else: Placing positive feelings within a general model of affect | Carver (2003), Cognition and Emotion 17(2):241–261. By its title, it places positive feelings in a control-process model of affect as a sign that one can attend to something else. Unread: registered so that the claim that positive affect releases a goal's priority, which bears against reading valence intensity as the potential's strength, is checked against the paper. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-23, not yet sought: named in the reading of Carver (2018) as the paper in which positive affect is said to lower a goal's priority, which would conflict with the record's reading of valence intensity as the strength of an ordering's potential ([CLAIM-440](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-440.md)). To be read before that clause is promoted. |
| [LIT-1446](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1446.md) | The dynamic architecture of emotion: Evidence for the component process model | Scherer (2009), Cognition and Emotion 23(7):1307–1351. The component process model's evidence review. Emotion is "an emergent, dynamic process based on an individual's subjective appraisal of significant events", and the paper gives special emphasis to the sequence of appraisal checks and the synchronisation of response systems. Unread: the model is read in the companion paper [LIT-1451](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1451.md). | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-23 from Crossref, not read: a lawful copy exists but this client could not reach it. The University of Geneva's Archive ouverte holds the published version (unige:97810), with access restricted to members of the UNIGE/HUG community. The Taylor & Francis article is paywalled. The Geneva E3 Lab's publications page posts many of the group's 2009 papers but not this one, and a web search found no other author or course posting. Its argument is read first-hand in Scherer's companion paper of the same year, "Emotions are emergent processes: they require a dynamic computational architecture" ([LIT-1451](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1451.md)), which restates the component process model and cites this paper, then in press, for the evidence. Filed because the record's proposal needs a measurable analogue of potential, and this is the review usually cited for response synchronization. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-1447](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1447.md) | EMA: A process model of appraisal dynamics | Marsella & Gratch (2009), Cognitive Systems Research 10(1):70–90. EMA (EMotion and Adaptation), after Smith and Lazarus. Appraisal is one fast, parallel, automatic process over the agent's causal interpretation, a decision-theoretic plan representation of its beliefs, desires, intentions and plans. Emotional dynamics come from the time course of the perception, inference and action that change that interpretation, so no multi-level appraisal is needed. Each proposition gets an appraisal frame. Frames compete for coping, and the most recently accessed one with the highest mood-adjusted intensity wins. Coping changes the world or the agent's beliefs, desires and intentions, which drives reappraisal. Illustrated with an actor's reaction to a pigeon. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1100](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1100.md)): in full, from the published version on a University of Kentucky course reading list, checked against the authors' manuscript on Gratch's USC page. Worth reading as the worked computational case of appraisal as a continuous process over the agent's causal interpretation, with an explicit arbitration rule. Appraisal is a single, fast, parallel mapping from that interpretation to appraisal variables. Its dynamics come from the slower perception, inference and action that change the interpretation, and from coping, which alters beliefs, desires and intentions and so drives reappraisal. Appraisal frames, one per proposition, compete for the coping response. The winner is the most recently accessed frame with the highest mood-adjusted intensity, and intensity is a decision-theoretic product of likelihood and utility. That is arbitration on a common currency among concerns, not a negotiation among perspectives. |
| [LIT-1448](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1448.md) | Back to Bentham? Explorations of Experienced Utility | Kahneman, Wakker & Sarin (1997), Quarterly Journal of Economics 112(2):375–405. "Utility" has two meanings: decision utility, an outcome's weight in choice, and experienced utility, its hedonic quality. Experienced utility is instant (the pleasure or distress of the moment, reported in real time) or remembered (a retrospective evaluation). Remembered utility follows the Peak-End average and neglects duration. Choices follow remembered utility, so subjects repeat a longer cold-water trial that dominates the shorter one in pain. Axioms on ordinal instant utility with a neutral zero make total utility the time integral of a value transform. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1105](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1105.md)): in full, from the published article as deposited in Erasmus University Rotterdam's repository (RePub, hdl 1765/23011). Distinguishes decision utility (an outcome's weight in choice) from experienced utility (hedonic quality). Experienced utility divides into instant utility, reported in real time, and remembered utility, a retrospective evaluation. Remembered utility follows a Peak-End rule and neglects duration. Choices follow remembered utility, so people choose dominated, longer painful episodes. Axioms on ordinal instant utility with a neutral zero yield total utility as a time integral. Filed for the record's three-layer operationalization of felt valence ([CLAIM-440](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-440.md)). |
| [LIT-1449](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1449.md) | Control Theory, Goal Attainment, and Psychopathology | Carver (2018), Psychological Inquiry 29(3):139–144, a commentary on DeYoung and Krueger. Problems arise wherever a feedback loop's input, reference value, comparison or output is extreme or biased. The five factors are read as sensitivities to classes of goals, not as loop parameters. Valence tracks the velocity of goal attainment against a reference value, so approach and avoidance can each yield either sign. Doubt and disengagement sit outside the loop itself. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1102](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1102.md)): in full, from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC6707771, NIHMS1512534). A short commentary on DeYoung and Krueger's cybernetic theory of psychopathology, and the nearest lawful first-hand statement found of Carver and Scheier's control-process account of affect. Valence is read off the velocity of goal attainment against a reference value. An approach system and an avoidance system can each produce either sign. Many goals are in play at once, and their priorities are juggled. It stands in for the unread 1990 paper ([LIT-1441](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1441.md)). |
| [LIT-1450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1450.md) | Pain experience in hermit crabs? | Elwood & Appel (2009), Animal Behaviour 77(5):1243–1246. Hermit crabs given small shocks inside their shells. Only shocked crabs evacuated, and fewer did so from a preferred shell species, which the authors read as a motivational trade-off. Crabs that stayed were later quicker to take a new shell. "The results are consistent with the idea of pain in these animals." Unread beyond the abstract. | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-23 from Crossref, not read beyond the abstract: no lawful full text could be reached. OpenAlex lists it as closed; Queen's University Belfast's research portal has the record and abstract but no file; the Elsevier article is paywalled; a web search found no author or course posting. Filed because it is one of the two hermit-crab trade-off studies usually cited for the criterion [THEORY-101](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-101.md)'s promotion names, an animal accepting a noxious cost for a resource, and the bumblebee study ([LIT-1466](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1466.md)) cites it as such. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-1451](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1451.md) | Emotions are emergent processes: they require a dynamic computational architecture | Scherer (2009), Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 364:3459–3474. Emotion is a bounded episode of synchronization among organismic subsystems, driven by a fixed sequence of appraisal checks (relevance, implications, coping, normative significance) and aimed at control precedence. The feeling component monitors the process by integrating a representation of all components and their coherence, and the degree of synchronization is hypothesised to generate conscious experience. Proposes nonlinear dynamic modelling: emotions as attractor basins of coupled oscillators, with hysteresis and cusp-catastrophe jumps. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1113](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1113.md)): in full, from the PubMed Central text (PMC2781886). Worth reading as Scherer's own compact statement of the component process model, the same year as the evidence review [LIT-1446](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1446.md), which it cites as in press. Emotion is a bounded episode of component synchronization, driven by sequential appraisal checks and aimed at control precedence. The feeling component monitors the process by representing the other components and their coherence. The degree of synchronization is hypothesised to generate conscious experience. Emotions are attractor basins of coupled oscillators, with hysteresis and catastrophe-surface jumps. It stands in for the unread review. |
| [LIT-1452](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1452.md) | Conscious emotional experience emerges as a function of multilevel, appraisal-driven response synchronization | Grandjean, Sander & Scherer (2008), Consciousness and Cognition 17(2):484–495. Componential appraisal models explain feelings better than basic-emotion or dimensional models. Appraisal runs in parallel at sensory-motor, schematic and conceptual levels and stops at the first conclusive result. Consciousness of an emotion emerges when lower levels cannot cope, especially when component synchronization reaches a critical level and duration, so that conscious, representational regulation is required. Conscious feeling needs, besides component synchronization, local and distant neuronal synchronization that integrates the components' representations. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1115](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1115.md)): in full, from the copy the authors' laboratory (the Geneva E3 Lab) posts on its publications page. Worth reading as the component process model's fullest account of when emotion becomes conscious. Appraisal runs in parallel at several levels and stops when a lower level reaches a conclusive result. Consciousness is recruited when it does not: when component synchronization reaches a critical level and duration that cannot be regulated automatically, so that higher-level regulation, which needs explicit representations, must take over. The feeling is a central representation built by neuronal synchronization, local and distant. Its measures are EEG gamma and beta activity in felt versus unfelt episodes, and phase coherence between brain regions. It partly rivals and partly supports the record's self-model condition for felt valence ([CLAIM-439](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-439.md)). |

The review that introduced the evaluative space model. Attitudes have been measured on one bipolar scale. The positive and negative evaluative processes behind them are separable, and can be activated reciprocally, independently or together. | [LIT-1455](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1455.md) | Bridging emotion theory and neurobiology through dynamic systems modeling | Lewis (2005), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 28(2):169–194, with open peer commentary. Appraisal and emotion are not cause and effect but constituents that organize one another, through positive and negative feedback and circular causality, into an emotion–appraisal amalgam, an "emotional interpretation". Trigger, self-amplification and self-stabilization phases. Interpretations are attractors, one converging at a time, with abrupt phase transitions between them. Their neural basis is nested corticolimbic loops, neuromodulation, vertical integration, action monitoring and theta-band synchrony, and stable states drive learning on a developmental timescale. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1119](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1119.md)): the target article in part, from the BBS treatment posted on the University of Geneva E3 Lab's publications page with Sander and Scherer's commentary. Worth reading as the fullest dynamic-systems account of appraisal and emotion. Appraisal and emotion constituents organize each other into one "emotional interpretation" through bidirectional feedback, in trigger, self-amplification and self-stabilization phases. Emotional interpretations are attractors, one at a time, and switch by phase transition. Vertical integration gives them momentum and selects among them. Stable states drive learning across a slower timescale. It contains the dynamics of one organization coming to prevail, but what prevails is an interpretation, not an ordering of the system's own states. |

The full statement of the evaluative space model for attitudes. Bipolar measures fold together states that a bivariate measure keeps apart, among them ambivalence (high positivity and negativity) and indifference (low both). | [LIT-1457](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1457.md) | The Emotion Process: Event Appraisal and Component Differentiation | Scherer & Moors (2019), Annual Review of Psychology 70:719–745. A review of experimental evidence on the emotion process, organised by five appraisal criteria (novelty, intrinsic and extrinsic valence, agency, control or power, fairness) and three paths from appraisal: to action tendencies, to physiological responses and to facial, vocal and gestural expression. Appraisal criteria have more stable response correlates than emotion categories do. Proposes that coherence among components above a threshold marks an episode, and above a second threshold awareness. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1106](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1106.md)): in full, from the PDF Annual Reviews serves to guest readers. Worth reading as the latest review of the component process model's evidence, organised by appraisal criterion rather than by emotion category. Its paths run from appraisal to action tendencies, to physiological responses and to expression. It separates intrinsic valence from goal congruence and reports the few studies that pull them apart: they have partly different physiological signatures and combine multiplicatively. It ends with a two-threshold proposal: coherence among components above one threshold starts an episode, and above a second it becomes aware. It does not describe appraisal as a negotiation among perspectives. |
| [LIT-1458](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1458.md) | Levels of valence | Shuman, Sander & Scherer (2013), Frontiers in Psychology 4:261. Valence exists at two levels. Micro-valences are the valenced outcomes of separate appraisal checks (pleasantness, goal conduciveness, power, self-congruence, moral goodness), and they can conflict, which explains mixed feelings. Macro-valence is one-dimensional, always present, and the common currency for choice. It is integrated from micro-valences and other inputs by rules ranging from weighted sums to lexicographic and elimination-by-aspects strategies. Intrinsic pleasantness and goal conduciveness are dissociable, citing Berridge. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1108](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1108.md)): in full, from the publisher's open-access PDF (Frontiers, CC licence). Worth reading as the component process model's own statement that valence is several things. Five appraisal checks are each valenced (pleasantness, goal conduciveness, power, self-congruence, moral goodness), and these "micro-valences" are integrated, by weighted sums or by lexicographic and elimination rules, into a one-dimensional "macro-valence" that serves as the common currency for choice. It separates intrinsic pleasantness from goal conduciveness and grounds the split in Berridge. It bears directly on the objection that the record's potential account tracks 'wanting', not 'liking' ([CLAIM-438](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-438.md)). |
| [LIT-1459](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1459.md) | Pleasure systems in the brain | Berridge & Kringelbach (2015), Neuron 86(3):646–664. Reward is three separable components: 'liking' (hedonic impact), 'wanting' (incentive salience) and learning. 'Liking' can be measured without report, by orofacial taste reactivity, which is homologous from rats to human infants. It is generated by cubic-millimetre opioid and endocannabinoid hotspots in nucleus accumbens, ventral pallidum and perhaps cortex and pons. Mesolimbic dopamine and most "pleasure electrodes" raise 'wanting' without raising 'liking'. Incentive sensitization makes an addict want a drug that has become less pleasant. Objective 'liking' can occur without any felt pleasure. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1110](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1110.md)): in full, from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC4425246, NIHMS664561). A review of the affective neuroscience of pleasure. Reward splits into 'liking' (hedonic impact), 'wanting' (incentive salience) and learning, with separable mechanisms. 'Liking' is measured without report by taste reactivity, which is homologous across rats, apes and newborn humans. It is generated by small opioid and endocannabinoid hotspots. Mesolimbic dopamine and most "pleasure electrodes" raise 'wanting' without raising 'liking'. Objective 'liking' can occur without felt pleasure. Filed for the record's account of valence as potential ([CLAIM-440](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-440.md)), which wanting-without-liking puts under pressure. |
| [LIT-1461](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1461.md) | Liking, wanting, and the incentive-sensitization theory of addiction | Berridge & Robinson (2016), American Psychologist 71(8):670–679. 'Wanting' (incentive salience, mesolimbic and dopamine-related) and 'liking' (hedonic impact, small opioid and endocannabinoid hotspots) are dissociable. Repeated, especially intermittent high-dose, drug use can sensitize the 'wanting' system, making it hyper-reactive to drug cues and contexts, lastingly and perhaps permanently, while 'liking' need not rise and may fall. Sensitized 'wanting' can oppose cognitive desire, run without report, and grow during abstinence. Its scope is said to extend, on emerging evidence, to behavioural addictions and to the compulsions of dopamine dysregulation syndrome. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1109](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1109.md)): in full, from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC5171207, NIHMS816820). Worth reading as the authors' own short statement, a quarter-century on, of the incentive-sensitization theory of addiction. Drugs, and perhaps unpredictable non-drug rewards, can make mesolimbic 'wanting' systems lastingly hyper-reactive to cues and contexts, and 'liking' need not rise with it. Sensitized 'wanting' can oppose a person's cognitive desire, operate without report, persist for years and grow during abstinence. It is a review of the authors' programme. Filed for the record's question whether potential of a proxy for maintenance is valence, and the form addiction and metric fixation share ([QUESTION-267](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-267.md)), to which it gives a mechanism on the personal side. |
| [LIT-1463](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1463.md) | Interaction and threshold effects of appraisal on componential patterns of emotion: A study using cross-cultural semantic data | Meuleman, Moors, Fontaine, Renaud & Scherer (2019), Emotion 19:425–442. Re-analyses the GRID cross-cultural data on the meaning of 24 emotion words (34 samples, 27 countries) to test whether appraisal acts on motivation, physiology and expression through interactions and nonlinear effects. PCA reduces items to 7 appraisal and 11 response factors. Multivariate adaptive regression splines (MARS) select third-order interactions and hinges. Goal compatibility is the main effect, agency and norm compatibility pure modifiers. The strong hierarchy of appraisal decision trees is not found. Simulated patterns matched to words form a coherent map. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1104](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1104.md)): in full, from the authors' accepted manuscript in Ghent University's repository (biblio.ugent.be 8560097). Worth reading as the one study here that tests whether appraisal acts on the other emotion components linearly. It re-analyses the GRID data, culturally shared semantic profiles of 24 emotion words rated in 34 samples from 27 countries. It fits multivariate adaptive regression splines from seven appraisal factors to eleven motivation, physiology and expression factors. Goal compatibility is the main effect. Agency and norm compatibility act only in interactions, and some responses need splines. Its "threshold effects" are hinges in a continuous piecewise-linear fit. The data are word meanings, not episodes, and have no time, so they cannot bear on continuity or hysteresis in choice. |

| [LIT-1466](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1466.md) | Motivational trade-offs and modulation of nociception in bumblebees | Gibbons, Versace, Crump, Baran & Chittka (2022), PNAS 119(31). Bumblebees chose between two 40% sucrose feeders, heated to 55 °C in the test phase, and two unheated alternatives of 10–40%. They avoided the heated feeders when the alternatives were also rich and fed from them more as the alternatives got poorer, guided by learned colour cues. The authors read this as a centrally mediated motivational trade-off, consistent with a capacity for pain. Corrected in 2025 for a misreported model. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1114](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1114.md)): in full, from the published version (CC BY 4.0) in LSE Research Online, with the 2025 correction and the authors' deposited data. Worth reading as the cleanest published motivational trade-off in an insect. Bees chose between heated (55 °C) and unheated feeders. They took the heated, high-sucrose feeders less as the unheated alternative got sweeter, and more steeply than when nothing was heated. The trade-off relied on learned colour cues, so it is central. At this one cost the data are graded, not thresholded, and the design varies only the resource, so it cannot show a threshold in cost. |

| [LIT-1468](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1468.md) | Deeply Felt Affect: The Emergence of Valence in Deep Active Inference | Hesp, Smith, Parr, Allen, Friston & Ramstead (2021), Neural Computation 33(2):398–446. Valence is a state of self, inferred at a hierarchically deeper level from changes in the expected precision γ of one's action model, which weights preference-driven expected free energy against a habitual prior in policy selection. The update to γ, affective charge, is positive when outcomes raise confidence in the action model and negative when they lower it. The valence level sends priors on γ back down. A simulated rat in a T-maze with context reversal infers negative and then positive valence, and adapts better than an agent without that level. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1111](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1111.md)): in full, from the publisher's CC BY PDF as deposited in Aarhus University's repository (pure.au.dk), checked against the University of Amsterdam deposit. A deep active-inference model of valence. A precision term γ sets how far the agent's preference-driven action model, rather than a habitual prior, governs policy selection. Its update, "affective charge", is positive when outcomes raise confidence in the action model and negative when they lower it. A second, slower level infers a binary valence state from affective charge and sends priors on γ back down. Simulated in a T-maze with reversal, the agent with the valence level adapts faster than one without it. "Felt" means explicitly represented, which the authors take as necessary for self-reportable experience of valence. Filed for the record's candidate that a valence regime is felt when the system models its own potential ([CLAIM-440](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-440.md)). |

DynAffect: individual differences in how feelings change over time come from three processes, an affective home base ("a baseline attractor state around which affect fluctuates"), variability in response to internal or external perturbation, and the attractor strength that ties affect back to the home base. | [LIT-1471](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1471.md) | An Appraisal-Driven Componential Approach to the Emotional Brain | Sander, Grandjean & Scherer (2018), Emotion Review 10:219–231. A perspective article. Major emotion theories agree that emotion has five components, so the emotional brain should be studied as five functionally defined networks: elicitation (appraisal), expression, autonomic reaction, action tendency and feeling. Appraisal drives the changes and the synchronization in the other four. Synchronization is proposed to be neuronal phase or cross-frequency coupling within and between components, and feeling to emerge when it passes a threshold. No measure is given and no data are reported. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1103](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1103.md)): in full, from the published version deposited in the Archive ouverte UNIGE (unige:109591). It splits the emotional brain into five functionally defined networks (elicitation, expression, autonomic reaction, action tendency, feeling). It proposes that component synchronization is neuronal phase or cross-frequency synchronization, within and between components, and repeats Scherer's hypothesis that feeling arises when the degree of synchronization passes a threshold. It names control precedence as priority among action tendencies. It gives no measure of synchronization and reports no data of its own. |

Many perceptions and cognitions impel action; the negative state of dissonance arises not from all cognitive conflict but when cognitions with action implications conflict, making it hard to act. | [LIT-1478](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1478.md) v2 | Routines die hard: Ontological security and audience agency in securitisation | Ku & Finch (2024). Alongside the political agency the Copenhagen School grants a securitising audience, drawing on Giddens they propose ontological agency: control over the stability of one's everyday routines, exercised to minimise disruption by securitisation. Because routines bracket anxiety, people may ignore securitising moves and emergency measures that would undermine ontological security. Unstructured observations of South Koreans' responses to military practices securitising North Korea show latent anxiety, ranging from inaction while routines are undisturbed to emotional outbursts when they are disrupted. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1133](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1133.md)) from the CC BY version of record; worth reading for the concept of ontological agency, an audience's maintenance of its routines, which often means ignoring securitisation rather than accepting or contesting it. Its South Korean illustration is chance observation of routine missile launches ignored in Gangneung, and tweets of fear and blame after a malfunction under a news embargo. The authors read the inaction as coping that lets securitisation reproduce itself, with anxiety latent and its management delegated to elites, not as resistance to the security narrative. |
| [LIT-1479](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1479.md) v2 | Anxiety as a disorder of uncertainty: implications for understanding maladaptive anxiety, anxious avoidance, and exposure therapy | Brown, Price & Dombrovski (2023; preprint 2022). A narrative review and proposal, with no new data or model run. Cognitive-behavioural accounts put exaggerated threat expectancy behind maladaptive anxiety, but the learning literature (seven computational studies, chosen without a systematic search) fits better a disorder of uncertainty learning: altered adjustment of learning rate to noise and volatility, mostly for aversive outcomes. They propose that in aversive settings avoidance of uncertain states keeps their uncertainty high and so perpetuates itself, that anxiety feeds this by misreading noise as change, and that exposure therapy works by reducing the uncertainty. For fear-based disorders, not GAD. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1120](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1120.md)) from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central, not the typeset version of record; worth reading as the clearest statement that anxious avoidance can be kept going by uncertainty that avoidance itself leaves unreduced, with no excess of learned threat needed. A narrative review and proposal: seven computational studies, chosen without a systematic search, show altered adjustment of learning rate to uncertainty, mostly for aversive outcomes; the avoidance loop and the account of exposure are argued in words and schematic figures, not modelled or tested. For fear-based disorders; by the authors' statement it does not explain GAD. |
